Unwittingly
un-WIT-ing-lee
adverb
From the Saxon witan, to know (whence wit, wot, wist), with the negative prefix — literally “not knowingly.” It renders the Hebrew bishgagah, in error or inadvertence, the standing legal term for sin committed without deliberate intent.

Biblical Definition

Unwittingly is one of the most searching words in the law, because it establishes that ignorance reduces guilt without abolishing it. If a man eat of the holy thing unwittingly, he must still restore it, and add the fifth part, and bring it to the priest (Lev 22:14) — the sin was unintentional, and there is still restitution and a sacrifice. The whole apparatus of the sin offering exists for exactly this class of transgression. The manslayer “that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly” may flee to the city of refuge (Josh 20:3), and there the mercy is real: he is not delivered into the hand of the avenger of blood, because he “smote his neighbour unwittingly” (Josh 20:5). But mark the limit of that mercy — he must run, and he must stay, and he is not free until the death of the high priest. Even innocent-of-intent blood confines a man to the refuge until a priest dies. This is the gospel written in the law: the unwitting sinner is not therefore a guiltless sinner, and his liberty waits upon the death of his High Priest. Our Lord’s own prayer stands over the whole doctrine — “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Luk 23:34). Not knowing did not make them innocent. It made them candidates for pardon.

Webster 1828 Definition

Without knowledge or intention; inadvertently. In the law, the term marking sin done in error, which still requires atonement and restitution.

expand to see more

UNWITTINGLY, adv. Without knowledge; without design or intention; inadvertently.

From un and witting, the participle of the obsolete verb wit, to know; Saxon witan.

Of the same family as wot, wist, and wit, all signifying knowledge.

In the Mosaic law, equivalent to the Hebrew bishgagah, in error (Lev 4:2; Lev 22:14).

Distinguished from sin committed presumptuously, or with a high hand (Num 15:30), for which no offering was appointed.

Key Scripture

Lev 22:14 — "And if a man eat of the holy thing unwittingly, then he shall put the fifth part thereof unto it, and shall give it unto the priest with the holy thing."

Josh 20:3 — "That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood."

Josh 20:5 — "And if the avenger of blood pursue after him, then they shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand; because he smote his neighbour unwittingly , and hated him not beforetime ."

Luk 23:34 — "Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots."

Modern Corruption

The modern rule that sincerity excuses — that no one is culpable for what he did not intend — is precisely the doctrine the sin offering was instituted to refute.

expand to see more

The corruption is the enthronement of intent. The age holds it self-evident that guilt attaches only to conscious malice: if a man did not mean it, he did not do it, and to hold him responsible is thought unjust. This makes conscience the measure of sin, and since a seared conscience feels least, the most hardened man becomes on this reckoning the most innocent. Scripture reasons the other way. The standard is the law of God, not the awareness of the sinner, and the sin offering exists because men constantly break a holy law without noticing. David prays to be cleansed from secret faults — faults secret from himself. If ignorance excused, the entire Levitical provision for sins of error would be a needless cruelty.

Recover the plain sense: the doctrine humbles and comforts at once. It humbles, because it means you are guilty of more than you can recall, and no examination of your own motives will ever certify you clean. It comforts, because God made public provision for exactly that guilt, and the provision was not a lower standard but a substitutionary death. The cities of refuge make the point unforgettably: real mercy, immediately available, freely given to the man who did not intend it — and full liberty only when the high priest dies. Christ is both the refuge the manslayer runs to and the priest whose death sets him free.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon witan, to know, negated — sin in ignorance, which the law treats as real guilt requiring real atonement.

expand to see more

Unwittingly — un + witting, from Saxon witan, to know.

Kin to wot, wist, and wit, the AV's other survivals of the same root.

Hebrew bishgagah, in error — the sin-offering category (Lev 4:2).

Opposed to sin done presumptuously, with a high hand (Num 15:30).

The manslayer’s freedom waits upon the death of the high priest (Josh 20:6).

Usage

"Lev 22:14: unintentional trespass still requires restitution with a fifth part added."

"Josh 20:3–5: real mercy for the unwitting, yet confinement until the high priest dies."

"Luk 23:34 shows ignorance as a ground for pleading pardon, never as a proof of innocence."
